To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the use of tamoxifen, raloxifine or aromatase inhibitor for breast cancer risk reduction is not recommended in women with a life expectancy of less than five years, (ii) tamoxifen or raloxifin is recommended in women with an increased risk for breast cancer (Gail model) and a life expectancy of at least five years, (iii) aromatase inhibitors are recommended in premenopausal women with an increased breast cancer risk and

the use of tamoxifen or raloxifine is associated with an absolute reduction in the incidence of breast cancer by 50% and a reduction of 70% in the incidence of invasive breast cancer in high-risk patients.

there is no proven effective chemoprevention for breast cancer.
chemoprevention of breast cancer is not indicated at present, although it may be indicated in the future for high-risk women.
there is no convincing evidence of a survival benefit of chemopreventive agents in breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of hormonal chemoprevention in women at increased risk for breast cancer is a reasonable option.
there is a need for more effective, better tolerated agents for breast cancer prevention, and that these should be evaluated in a more appropriate population.
the use of chemopreventive agents is limited to women who are at a very high risk for breast cancer and who are not at risk for other cancers or cardiovascular diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current evidence for the medical prevention of breast cancer is limited.
chemoprevention is not a one-size-fits-all approach.
the current evidence is insufficient to support the use of tamoxifen, raloxifrene, or aromatase-inhibitors for breast cancer prevention.
